SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models

Jiachun Jin    Zetong Zhou    Haonan Wang    Xiao Yang    Jun Zhu    Zhijie Deng Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

1 Introduction

Embodied foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models, connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, offering a path toward general-purpose robot control (Black et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). Their generalization depends on diverse interaction experience across tasks, objects, and environments, yet collecting such data through robot teleoperation remains costly. Egocentric human videos provide a complementary source of experience, capturing everyday manipulation without requiring robot hardware or teleoperation (Grauman et al., 2022; Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026). Using this experience for policy learning, however, requires bridging the human-to-robot embodiment gap: the same operation can involve different motions and control mechanisms across humans and robots, and is often performed in scenes that differ from the robot’s workspace.

Latent action models (LAMs) are a popular way to incorporate human videos into robot policy training without explicit action labels (Ye et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; Bu et al., 2025). By encoding visual transitions in a shared latent space, they provide a common prediction target for human and robot experience. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), which predict future video frames together with actions (Wu et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b), LAMs avoid explicit pixel prediction during policy learning, which can make training more efficient. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which constrains each latent to explain the transition within its own clip but does not relate human and robot executions of the same behavior. Their latents therefore tend to cluster by visual appearance, such as the scene, rather than by the underlying action, so semantically similar human and robot actions need not lie close together. Aligning human actions with their robot counterparts thus requires supervision that connects their meanings across embodiments.

Our insight is that language can provide this supervision. Even when human and robot clips are unpaired, natural-language descriptions of their atomic actions, such as “grasp the cup”, relate a human clip to multiple robot clips with different degrees of semantic similarity, as illustrated on the left of figure 1. We propose SALA, which trains a latent action tokenizer by translating these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents. Robot latents, grounded in control by action reconstruction, serve as anchors, and the alignment moves only human latents toward them. As the middle of figure 1 shows, the resulting latent actions are organized by action semantics rather than by scene, giving human videos a prediction target that is meaningful for robot control.

Once trained, the tokenizer labels videos from their frames alone, so its latent actions provide a unified supervision signal for training the policy on both human and robot videos, without action labels or atomic-action descriptions. This makes human video a scalable source of supervision along two axes. In pre-training, the policy can absorb large-scale general human videos spanning diverse everyday tasks. In post-training, because human and robot latent actions are aligned, task-specific human videos, i.e., human demonstrations of the target task, supervise the same action expert that controls the robot. Since such demonstrations require no robot, they offer a practical way to improve a policy on a new task, one that robot-only policies cannot exploit.

We evaluate SALA in simulation and on a real robot. On RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025b), where videos of another robot arm stand in for human videos, SALA achieves a higher average success rate than existing LAMs and WAMs trained on the same videos, with the largest gain in domain-randomized scenes. Analyses of the tokenizer show that language alignment organizes latent actions by atomic action semantics rather than by scene. On a real robot controlled in a 63-DoF action space, including two 22-DoF dexterous hands, human video helps along both axes. Pre-training on more general human video, up to 2,678 hours, consistently reduces the robot’s action prediction error on downstream tasks without additional robot data. With teleoperated demonstrations fixed, post-training on more task-specific human video raises the average real-robot success rate from 53.75% to 72.5%. The right of figure 1 shows both trends.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We use language as relational supervision: atomic-action descriptions align human and robot latent actions from unpaired videos, with the alignment anchored on robot latents grounded in control.

  • •

    We turn human videos into latent-action supervision for the same action expert that controls the robot, which enables scaling along two axes: general human video in pre-training and task-specific human video in post-training.

  • •

    Experiments in simulation and on a 63-DoF real robot with dexterous hands show that SALA outperforms prior LAMs and WAMs trained on the same cross-embodiment videos in average success rate, and that human video scales along both axes: more general human video in pre-training keeps reducing the robot’s action prediction error, and more task-specific human video in post-training raises real-world success rates.

2 Method

Our goal is to use action-free egocentric human videos, which can be collected at scale, to facilitate the training of robot policies. We connect these videos to robot control through latent actions. This connection requires latent actions to establish semantic correspondence across embodiments, which a shared latent space trained only by reconstructing each clip does not guarantee. As outlined in figure 2, SALA therefore learns a latent action tokenizer aligned across embodiments by language supervision from atomic-action descriptions, and uses it to leverage human videos in robot policy training.

2.1 Preliminaries: Latent Action Models

LAMs learn compact representations of visual transitions without action labels by coupling inverse and forward dynamics (Zhang et al., 2025a). Given observations 𝐨t\mathbf{o}_{t} and 𝐨t+k\mathbf{o}_{t+k} separated by a horizon kk, an inverse-dynamics encoder infers a latent action 𝐳=ℰθ​(𝐨t,𝐨t+k){\mathbf{z}=\mathcal{E}_{\theta}(\mathbf{o}_{t},\mathbf{o}_{t+k})} that encodes the transition between the two observations. An information bottleneck produces 𝐳~=𝒬ϕ​(𝐳){\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}=\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}(\mathbf{z})}, limiting how much information from the future observation reaches the decoder. The forward-dynamics decoder 𝒢v\mathcal{G}_{v} then reconstructs 𝐨t+k\mathbf{o}_{t+k} from the current observation 𝐨t\mathbf{o}_{t} and the compressed code 𝐳~\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}. Training minimizes the reconstruction error in image or feature space over observed pairs.

The inferred codes can serve as prediction targets for policy learning from action-free videos (Ye et al., 2024; Bu et al., 2025). Their usefulness, however, depends on what they encode: accurate reconstruction does not guarantee that the latent captures controllable actions, since it may also retain scene information or changes unrelated to control (Zhang et al., 2025a). For human-to-robot transfer, the representation must additionally connect semantically related behaviors across embodiments, a relation that reconstruction within individual clips does not explicitly constrain. We therefore augment this predictive formulation with robot action supervision and language-guided cross-embodiment alignment.

2.2 Grounding Latent Actions in Robot Control

We train the latent action tokenizer on a human dataset 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} and an independently collected robot dataset 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}}:

𝒟H={(ViH,ℓiH)}i=1NH,𝒟R={(VjR,ℓjR,𝐬j,𝐚j)}j=1NR.{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}}=\{(V_{i}^{H},\ell_{i}^{H})\}_{i=1}^{N_{H}},\quad{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}}=\{(V_{j}^{R},\ell_{j}^{R},\mathbf{s}_{j},\mathbf{a}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N_{R}}. (2.1)

Each clip V=(𝐨t,𝐨t+k)V=(\mathbf{o}_{t},\mathbf{o}_{t+k}) is represented by its endpoint observations, and 𝐬\mathbf{s} and 𝐚\mathbf{a} are the initial robot state and the subsequent action chunk, available only for robot data. The natural-language description ℓ\ell specifies the atomic actions performed by the embodiment in the clip. As shown in figure 2(a), human and robot clips share the visual encoder ℰθ\mathcal{E}_{\theta}, the quantizer 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}, and the visual decoder 𝒢v\mathcal{G}_{v}, trained with visual reconstruction losses as in section 2.1.

Visual reconstruction alone does not ensure that the latent captures controllable actions. Teleoperation data, however, already provide ground-truth robot actions, which we exploit during tokenizer training. A robot-only action decoder 𝒢a\mathcal{G}_{a} reconstructs the action chunk 𝐚\mathbf{a} from 𝐳~\widetilde{\mathbf{z}} and the initial state 𝐬\mathbf{s}, with loss ℒact\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}, which grounds robot latents directly in control (Chen et al., 2026b). Human clips share this space without action labels; the control-grounded robot latents later serve as anchors for cross-embodiment alignment.

2.3 Robot-Anchored Semantic Transfer

We align human latent actions toward the robot representations grounded by action reconstruction in section 2.2. These robot representations serve as control anchors, while atomic-action descriptions determine how each human clip should relate to them.

Atomic-action descriptions characterize what a clip does independently of the embodiment performing it. We therefore encode ℓ\ell with a frozen text encoder and use the similarity between language descriptions to measure how semantically related a human clip is to each robot clip. Because human and robot clips are collected independently, a human clip rarely has an exact robot counterpart. It can nonetheless relate to several robot clips to different degrees; for example, grasping a cup is closer to grasping a bottle than to placing a cup. We therefore describe each human clip by a soft neighborhood over the robot clips in a batch, given by a softmax over its language similarities, and use it to supervise the clip’s neighborhood in latent space. Figure 2(a) illustrates this with SℓS^{\ell} and SzS^{z}, the language and latent similarities between the human and robot clips in a batch: the dashed rows give the two neighborhoods of one human clip. Formally, the alignment loss is

ℒalign=𝔼i​[CE⁡(softmaxj⁡(si​jℓ)⏟Pi,softmaxj⁡(si​jz)⏟Qi)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\mathbb{E}_{i}\Big[\operatorname{CE}\big(\underbrace{\operatorname{softmax}_{j}(s^{\ell}_{ij})}_{P_{i}},\,\underbrace{\operatorname{softmax}_{j}(s^{z}_{ij})}_{Q_{i}}\big)\Big], (2.2)

where si​jℓs^{\ell}_{ij} and si​jzs^{z}_{ij} are the entries of SℓS^{\ell} and SzS^{z} for human clip ii and robot clip jj, with si​jz=sim⁡(𝐳iH,sg⁡(𝐳jR))s^{z}_{ij}=\operatorname{sim}(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{H},\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{z}_{j}^{R})); the softmax temperatures are omitted for clarity. Here sim\operatorname{sim} denotes cosine similarity averaged over tokens, and the stop-gradient sg\operatorname{sg} makes alignment move human latents toward the control-grounded robot anchors rather than pulling the anchors toward human latents, which lack action supervision. Language thus supervises what visual and action reconstruction leave unconstrained: the semantic correspondence between human and robot latent actions.

The choice of quantizer matters for this alignment. The relations in PiP_{i} are graded, so alignment needs to move the pre-quantization latents 𝐳\mathbf{z} continuously, while the policy’s targets are the tokens that 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} produces from them. A standard hard VQ (van den Oord et al., 2017) fits these graded relations poorly: its commitment loss pulls each 𝐳\mathbf{z} toward the selected codeword, and its token, a one-hot assignment to a single codeword, changes only when 𝐳\mathbf{z} switches to another code. We therefore instantiate 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} with SoftVQ (Chen et al., 2025a), which represents each token as a categorical distribution over the codebook rather than a one-hot assignment, and forms 𝐳~\widetilde{\mathbf{z}} from the codewords weighted by these distributions; we denote the tokens of a clip by 𝐲\mathbf{y}. SoftVQ requires no commitment loss, and its distributions vary smoothly with 𝐳\mathbf{z}, so the tokens can express graded differences between latents. As shown in section 3.4, the alignment loss decreases with SoftVQ but stays near its initial value with hard VQ.

The tokenizer is trained with the three signals described above: visual reconstruction of human and robot clips (ℒvisH\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}}^{H} and ℒvisR\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}}^{R}) captures visual transitions, action reconstruction (ℒact\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}) grounds robot latents in control, and semantic alignment (ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}) supervises the correspondence between human and robot latents. With loss weights λact\lambda_{\mathrm{act}} and λalign\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}, the overall objective is

ℒtok=12​(ℒvisH+ℒvisR)+λact​ℒact+λalign​ℒalign.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}}^{H}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}}^{R}\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{act}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}. (2.3)

2.4 Latent-Action-Supervised Policy Learning

After training, the tokenizer is frozen and serves as a teacher that labels human and robot clips with latent actions. For a clip (𝐨t,𝐨t+k)(\mathbf{o}_{t},\mathbf{o}_{t+k}), the teacher outputs its latent action tokens 𝐲\mathbf{y}, each a categorical distribution over the codebook. We keep these distributions rather than discretizing them into code indices, retaining the graded similarity structure of the latent space. The future observation 𝐨t+k\mathbf{o}_{t+k} is used only to compute 𝐲\mathbf{y}; the policy itself observes only the current observation, so neither the teacher nor future frames are needed at deployment.

As shown in figure 2(b), our policy adopts a π0\pi_{0}-style architecture (Black et al., 2024): a vision-language model (VLM) encodes observations and language, and an action expert generates action chunks by flow matching. We add learnable latent-action queries to the action expert, which predict the token distributions 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}} through a latent head, and let the noisy action tokens attend to these queries, so that latent-action prediction directly conditions action generation. For human videos, which provide neither states nor actions, the action expert processes only the latent queries.

Both human and robot data are supervised by the latent-action loss ℒLA=𝔻KL(𝐲∥𝐲^)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LA}}=\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbf{y}\,\|\,\hat{\mathbf{y}}), the KL divergence between the teacher’s and the predicted categorical distributions over the codebook, averaged over tokens; robot data additionally contribute the flow-matching action loss ℒFMR\mathcal{L}^{R}_{\mathrm{FM}}:

ℒpolicy=ℒFMR+λLA​(ℒLAR+ℒLAH).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{policy}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{R}+\lambda_{\mathrm{LA}}\big(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LA}}^{R}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LA}}^{H}\big). (2.4)

Human videos thus train the same VLM and action expert that generate robot actions.

We train the policy in stages that follow the availability of data. In pre-training, the policy learns from the action-free videos in 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} with ℒLAH\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LA}}^{H} alone, predicting the latent actions that the language-aligned teacher assigns to them. Since the teacher requires only video frames, this stage needs neither action labels nor atomic-action descriptions, and can therefore scale with the amount of available human video. In mid-training, it is trained on target-robot teleoperation data 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} with ℒFMR+λLA​ℒLAR\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{R}+\lambda_{\mathrm{LA}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LA}}^{R}, grounding these latent-action predictions in robot actions. When task-specific data are available, an optional post-training stage uses both task-specific teleoperated and human demonstrations with the full objective in equation 2.4. Human demonstrations of the target task are cheap to collect, since they require no robot, and the aligned latent space lets them supervise the same action expert that controls the robot. Each experiment in section 3 specifies which stages it uses and on which data; architectural details and loss weights are given in section 8.

3 Experiments

Our experiments test the central claim of SALA: language-aligned latent actions turn videos of other embodiments into supervision for robot policies that is both effective and scalable. After summarizing the implementation in section 3.1, we evaluate the two properties in turn. For effectiveness, section 3.2 compares SALA on a standardized simulation benchmark with existing LAMs and WAMs trained on the same cross-embodiment videos. For scalability, section 3.3 asks whether SALA keeps improving the target robot in the real world as more human video is used, both with increasing human-video pre-training budgets and in task-specific post-training. We then ablate the design choices of our tokenizer and analyze whether its latent actions are aligned across embodiments in section 3.4.

3.1 Implementation Details

We summarize the main configuration here. The tokenizer encodes each clip, whose two observations are separated by a dataset-specific horizon kk, into 8 latent tokens, quantized by SoftVQ with a codebook of 256 codes; visual reconstruction targets frozen DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) features of the future observation, and atomic-action descriptions are embedded by a frozen text encoder, CLIP ViT-B/32 in simulation and Qwen3-Embedding-4B (Zhang et al., 2025b) in the real world. The policy uses Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025) as the VLM and a separately parameterized Qwen3-style transformer with 0.6B parameters as the action expert, which attends jointly with the VLM at every layer. The VLM is initialized from the pretrained Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct weights and the action expert from scratch, and each subsequent training stage starts from the checkpoint of the previous one. Experiment-specific tokenizer settings, loss weights, and further architectural details are given in section 8.

3.2 Effectiveness in Simulation

We first compare SALA with existing approaches to cross-embodiment video pre-training on a standardized simulation benchmark. Specifically, we ask whether, given the same videos of a non-target embodiment, SALA achieves higher target-robot success rates than other LAMs and WAMs.

Setup.

We conduct this comparison on RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025b), a bimanual manipulation benchmark that provides expert trajectories for 50 dual-arm tasks across five robot embodiments. We take Aloha-AgileX as the target embodiment and ARX-X5 as the non-target embodiment. As listed in table 2 and illustrated in figure 11, 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} keeps only the videos of 27,000 ARX-X5 trajectories from both clean and random scenes, whereas 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} contains only 2,500 complete Aloha-AgileX trajectories from clean scenes. This order-of-magnitude gap mimics the practical regime in which target-robot data are scarce while videos of other embodiments are abundant. Clips in both datasets are further annotated with atomic-action descriptions, which are used only to train our tokenizer; the annotation procedure and examples are given in section 9. We evaluate on Aloha-AgileX in both the clean and domain-randomized settings of the benchmark, denoted Clean and Random. In each setting, we run 100 rollouts per task and report the success rate averaged over all 50 tasks.

Training.

The tokenizer is trained on 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} and 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} with equation 2.3, where only Aloha-AgileX clips contribute action reconstruction. Following section 2.4, the policy is then pre-trained on the ARX-X5 videos to predict latent actions only, and mid-trained on 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} with both the flow-matching action loss and the latent-action loss. We omit task-specific post-training in this setting. The tokenizer settings of this experiment are listed in table 7.

Baselines.

We compare with three types of baselines: (i) VLAs, i.e., π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) and X-VLA (Zheng et al., 2025), trained on 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} only; (ii) WAMs, i.e., FastWAM (Yuan et al., 2026b), LingBot-VA (Li et al., 2026b), InternVLA-A1.5 (Ma et al., 2026), and OpenWAM (Wang et al., 2026), additionally trained with their future-prediction objectives on 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} and 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}}; and (iii) LAMs, i.e., UniVLA (Bu et al., 2025), UniT (Chen et al., 2026a), and RotVLA (Li et al., 2026c), additionally trained to predict latent actions on 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} and 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}}.

Results.

SALA achieves the highest success rate in Random and the highest average in table 2. Although it is initialized only from a general-purpose VLM, it outperforms every baseline initialized from a robot-pretrained checkpoint. None of the other LAMs relates the two embodiments through action semantics, so an ARX-X5 latent and an Aloha-AgileX latent need not encode the same action; what their policies learn from 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} may therefore not transfer to Aloha-AgileX. SALA aligns ARX-X5 latents to Aloha-AgileX latents grounded in control, so pre-training on 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} supervises the action expert with targets that are meaningful for Aloha-AgileX control. Three of the four WAMs instead predict future videos, a target that also requires modeling scene appearance, whereas InternVLA-A1.5 predicts latent foresight tokens rather than pixels. Consistent with this, FastWAM and OpenWAM match or exceed SALA in Clean but collapse in Random, where domain randomization changes scene appearance. In contrast, section 3.4 shows that language-aligned latent actions are organized by action semantics rather than by scene.

3.3 Scalability in the Real World

We next deploy SALA on a real robot to study how it scales with egocentric human videos. We examine two levels: scaling human-video pre-training to 2,678 equivalent hours, and scaling human demonstrations of each downstream task in post-training.

Setup.

All real-world experiments are conducted on a Sharpa North wheeled humanoid equipped with two 22-DoF Sharpa Wave dexterous hands, whose 63-dimensional joint-space action covers the arms, hands, torso, and neck; section 10 details the platform. As summarized in table 2, we use action-free egocentric human videos 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} for 2,678 equivalent hours of pre-training, alongside 888 hours of robot teleoperation data 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}}. Each downstream task further pairs a limited set of teleoperated demonstrations 𝒟Rtask{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}^{\mathrm{task}}} with human demonstrations 𝒟Htask{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}^{\mathrm{task}}}, egocentric videos of a person performing the same task; figure 3 shows the large-scale data on the left and these demonstrations on the right. Teleoperated demonstrations supply the task’s robot actions, but they are costly to collect and hard to scale. Human demonstrations carry no actions, but since they require no robot, they are cheap to collect and easy to scale. As in simulation, atomic-action descriptions are used only for tokenizer training, so we annotate only the data used to train it: 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} and a subset 𝒟Htok⊂𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}^{\mathrm{tok}}}\subset{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}}, while pre-training on the full 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} requires no annotation.

Downstream tasks.

We evaluate four downstream manipulation tasks: gear assembly, bimanual pouring, flower insertion, and spoon scooping, the last of which requires tool use. Table 4 summarizes each task and the teleoperated and human demonstrations collected for it, and section 11 gives further details.

Training.

The tokenizer is trained on 𝒟Htok{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}^{\mathrm{tok}}} and 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} with equation 2.3. Following the full recipe of section 2.4, the policy is pre-trained on 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}} to predict latent actions only, and mid-trained on 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} with both the flow-matching action loss and the latent-action loss. It is then post-trained for each task on 𝒟Rtask{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}^{\mathrm{task}}} and 𝒟Htask{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}^{\mathrm{task}}} together, with the human demonstrations supervising latent-action prediction only. The tokenizer settings of this experiment are listed in table 7.

Main results.

We compare SALA with two baselines, both post-trained on the same teleoperated demonstrations 𝒟Rtask{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}^{\mathrm{task}}}: GR00T N1.7 (NVIDIA et al., 2025) and a vanilla VLA, which shares our architecture but removes latent actions, so it is trained on teleoperation data only and cannot learn from human videos. SALA uses human videos in both pre-training and post-training. As shown in table 4, SALA achieves the highest average success rate of 72.5%, surpassing the baselines on every task. Since the vanilla VLA differs from SALA only in latent actions, the gap between them measures what latent actions and the human videos they enable contribute. We next examine the two stages at which human videos enter, pre-training and post-training, in figure 4.

Scaling in pre-training.

Human videos provide an additional axis for scaling policy training beyond robot demonstrations. We pre-train the policy with budgets equivalent to 0, 473, 1,103, and 2,678 hours of human video, and then mid-train each for one epoch over the teleoperation data 𝒟R{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}} and post-train it on each task for 30,000 iterations. We report the validation L1 error between predicted and ground-truth actions on held-out teleoperated demonstrations of the four tasks, counting only the joints each task uses. We also compare with a vanilla VLA, which shares our architecture but removes latent actions; it is therefore trained on teleoperation data only and cannot learn from human videos, with all other settings unchanged. As shown in figure 4(a), the validation L1 error decreases with every increase in the pre-training budget. This improvement requires no additional robot data, since all models share the same teleoperation data in mid- and post-training.

Latent actions help even without human-video pre-training: our 0 h variant already achieves a lower final validation L1 error than the vanilla VLA. Because the latent actions are grounded in robot control, predicting them shapes the representations from which the action expert generates actions, and they let the human demonstrations of each task supervise the same action expert, which the vanilla VLA cannot exploit. With 2,678 hours of human-video pre-training, the error drops further below both the vanilla VLA and our 0 h variant, with the relative reductions marked in figure 4(a). Aligned latent actions thus let human video improve robot action prediction at both stages, through large-scale pre-training and through task-specific post-training.

Scaling in post-training.

At the task level, starting from the model pre-trained on 2,678 hours of human video, we post-train each of the four tasks with 10%, 50%, and 100% of its human demonstrations 𝒟Htask{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}^{\mathrm{task}}} while keeping the teleoperated demonstrations 𝒟Rtask{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.2109,0.7617}\mathcal{D}_{R}^{\mathrm{task}}} fixed. As shown in figure 4(b), the average success rate increases steadily with more human demonstrations, from 53.75% to 72.5%. Since human demonstrations require no robot to record, collecting more of them for a task offers an inexpensive way to improve the policy on that task, complementary to teleoperation.

3.4 Ablations and Analysis

We examine the robot-anchored semantic transfer described in section 2.3 in two steps. We first ablate the alignment loss and analyze what it contributes to the latent space, within a single embodiment and across embodiments; we then ablate two designs that determine how alignment acts, the stop-gradient that keeps robot latents as control anchors and the SoftVQ quantizer.

Semantic alignment.

This ablation tests whether the correspondence between human and robot latent actions needs explicit supervision or emerges from reconstruction alone. Since reconstruction constrains each latent only through its own clip, ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} is the only term in equation 2.3 that relates the two embodiments; we set λalign=0\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}=0 and keep everything else unchanged. As shown in table 5, removing alignment lowers success rates in both settings, so reconstruction alone does not provide this correspondence. The drop is larger in Random, where scenes vary. Figure 5 examines the ARX-X5 latents, which can be organized by scene as well as by action since the videos are recorded in both clean and randomized scenes. Without alignment, the clips of three of the four tasks in figure 5(a) split by scene, with the two actions mixed in each group; with alignment, they split by atomic action, since clips with semantically similar descriptions receive similar alignment targets regardless of the scene. As shown in figure 5(b), across all analyzed pairs, alignment raises the median fraction of latent variance explained by the action from 0.41 to 0.67 and lowers that explained by the scene from 0.14 to 0.04.

Cross-embodiment retrieval.

Figure 5 concerns clips of a single embodiment; we next test whether alignment also relates clips across embodiments. Given a query clip of a non-target embodiment, we retrieve the target-robot clips whose latent actions are most similar to it, searching over all tasks with the similarity used by the alignment loss. Figure 6 shows human queries from the pre-training videos 𝒟H{\color[rgb]{0.9,0.45,0.05}\mathcal{D}_{H}}, of tasks absent from the robot data. Human and robot videos differ in viewpoint, embodiment, and background, and the reconstruction-only tokenizer returns robot clips unrelated to the query. SALA instead returns semantically related robot behaviors; for example, a human sweeping the floor retrieves the robot sweeping trash into a dustpan. Section 6 evaluates retrieval quantitatively on RoboTwin 2.0 and in the real world.

Stop-gradient.

The stop-gradient makes alignment one-way: robot latents serve as fixed targets, and only human latents move toward them. Removing sg\operatorname{sg} from si​jzs^{z}_{ij} in equation 2.2 makes alignment bidirectional, so robot latents are also pulled toward human latents, which lack action supervision. Robot latents then have to serve two objectives, encoding the robot’s own actions and matching human latents, and the second can compromise the first. As shown in table 5, bidirectional alignment lowers success rates, most notably in the clean setting, indicating that robot latents should remain anchored to control.

Quantizer.

To test the choice of quantizer in section 2.3, we replace SoftVQ with a standard hard VQ. Figure 7 shows that SoftVQ substantially reduces the alignment loss, whereas hard VQ keeps it near the value of a uniform prediction, even though both reach comparable visual reconstruction losses. Since the alignment loss is computed on the pre-quantization latents, hard VQ hinders alignment already before quantization, consistent with the argument in section 2.3.

4 Related Work

Vision-language-action models.

VLA models build on pre-trained vision-language models to map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026a). Their generalization depends on the diversity of robot data, which is costly to collect through teleoperation. Language has also been used to structure action learning in VLAs, through interpretable action primitives (Weng et al., 2026) or language-conditioned action priors learned without visual input (Lin et al., 2026). SALA keeps the VLA design, with a flow-matching action expert, and adds latent-action prediction so that videos without action labels can supervise the same action expert.

Learning from human videos.

Human videos have been used to pre-train visual representations for robot manipulation (Nair et al., 2022). Closer to policy learning, one line of work extracts explicit motion from human videos, such as hand trajectories or poses, and maps it to robot actions (Wang et al., 2023; Kareer et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025); this requires hand tracking and a correspondence between human and robot kinematics.

With sufficiently diverse pre-training, co-training VLAs on such human data can yield human-to-robot transfer (Kareer et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026). Another line predicts future observations as a proxy for actions: generating video plans that are then converted into actions (Du et al., 2023; Ko et al., 2023), predicting subgoal images (Zhao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026), or training WAMs that predict videos jointly with actions (Wu et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b; NVIDIA et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Other work predicts future representations rather than pixels (Su et al., 2026; Miao et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026); when co-training on egocentric human videos, feature and 3D-flow targets transfer to robots better than pixel targets (Li et al., 2026a). Video prediction requires modeling scene appearance in addition to motion, and in section 3.2 some WAMs degrade sharply under domain randomization. SALA instead supervises the policy with latent actions, which require neither hand tracking nor pixel-level prediction.

Latent action models.

Instead of labeling videos with an inverse dynamics model trained on action-labeled data (Baker et al., 2022), latent action models infer actions from consecutive frames without action labels, by learning latents that predict the next frame (Schmidt and Jiang, 2023; Bruce et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Liang et al., 2026). They have been used to pre-train policies on actionless videos, including human videos (Ye et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; Bu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026c). Because the latents are learned by reconstructing each clip, they can capture scene changes and distractors rather than the action (Zhang et al., 2025a). Prior work addresses this by conditioning on task instructions (Bu et al., 2025), by structuring the latent space (Li et al., 2026c), by contrastive disentanglement with action-category priors (Dai et al., 2026), or by adversarially suppressing embodiment- and environment-specific factors (Liu et al., 2026). To relate embodiments, other methods align latents with robot actions recorded alongside the videos (Zhang et al., 2026a; Fan et al., 2026), with action labels of human hands (Luo et al., 2026), through paired human-robot demonstrations (Zhu et al., 2026), or through the shared visual consequences of heterogeneous kinematics (Chen et al., 2026a); a related approach contrastively aligns the action spaces of human hands, dexterous hands, and grippers (Bauer et al., 2026). SALA instead uses atomic-action descriptions to relate unpaired human and robot clips by graded semantic similarity, and aligns human latents to robot latents grounded in control, so that human and robot executions of semantically similar actions receive similar latents.

5 Conclusion

We presented SALA, which uses language to align human and robot latent actions for policy learning. Natural-language descriptions of atomic actions relate unpaired human and robot clips through graded semantic similarity, and SALA turns these relations into soft neighborhood targets that move human latents toward robot latents grounded in control. The resulting latent actions let human videos supervise the same action expert that controls the robot, both in large-scale pre-training and in task-specific post-training. Experiments in simulation and on a 63-DoF real robot show that language alignment organizes latent actions by action semantics rather than by scene, and that human-video pre-training steadily reduces the robot’s action prediction error without additional robot data.

Our study has limitations that point to future work. The tokenizer requires atomic-action descriptions for its training clips, although the policy itself learns from video frames alone. Our scaling analysis measures offline validation error with one run per setting and covers pre-training budgets of up to 2,678 hours; whether the trend continues at larger scales and how it translates into real-robot success remain open.

6 Cross-Embodiment Retrieval

Protocol.

As in section 3.4, each query clip of a non-target embodiment retrieves the most similar target-robot clip over all tasks, using the similarity of the alignment loss, i.e., the cosine similarity between pre-quantization latents 𝐳\mathbf{z} averaged over tokens. Besides the reconstruction-only tokenizer and SALA, we report two references: Random, a uniformly sampled robot clip, and Language, which retrieves by the similarity of atomic-action descriptions. On RoboTwin 2.0, ARX-X5 clips from 47 tasks query all Aloha-AgileX clips; we check whether the retrieved clip performs the same atomic action and measure the distance between the end-effector displacements of the two clips. In the real world, human clips query all robot teleoperation clips. For queries from the 56 tasks shared with the robot data, we check whether the retrieved clip comes from the same task and whether both hands perform the same verbs. For these queries and for those from tasks absent from the robot data, we also compute the similarity between the atomic-action descriptions of the query and the retrieved clip, rescaled so that Random scores 0 and Language scores 1.

Results.

Alignment improves every metric in table 6. On RoboTwin 2.0, the two embodiments share the viewpoint and workspace, so reconstruction alone already retrieves the same atomic action for 41.3% of queries; alignment raises this to 78.2%, with gains in all 47 tasks. In the real world, human and robot videos differ in viewpoint, embodiment, and background, and reconstruction alone is close to random. Alignment raises the same-task rate from 3.8% to 34.2%, and its language similarity on tasks absent from the robot data (0.31) is close to that on shared tasks (0.32). Figure 9 shows annotated examples of such tasks; for instance, a human sweeping the floor with a broom retrieves the robot sweeping trash into a dustpan.

7 Latent-Space Analysis of Semantic Alignment

Figure 5(a) shows that language alignment reorganizes ARX-X5 latents by atomic action rather than by scene type, i.e., clean or randomized. Figure 10 illustrates this change by clustering the latents of three pairs in figure 5(a) into two groups: without alignment, the two clusters are exactly the 40 clean and the 40 randomized clips, whereas with alignment, each cluster contains exactly one atomic action with 20 clips from each scene type.

8 Implementation Details

Tokenizer.

Table 7 lists the tokenizer settings of both experiments. Each observation is resized to 224×224224\times 224 and encoded by a frozen DINOv2-L, using features from its second-to-last layer. The visual encoder, a transformer with 8 layers and 16 heads, maps the endpoint features of a clip to 8 latent tokens. The quantizer is SoftVQ with 256 codes and a softmax temperature of 0.25. The visual decoder, also with 8 layers, predicts the DINOv2 features of the future observation, and the action decoder predicts the action chunk from the quantized latents and the initial robot state with a Huber loss (δ=0.35\delta=0.35). The visual reconstruction loss has weight 1, and the softmax temperature of QiQ_{i} in equation 2.2 is 0.2. To provide robot clips as alignment targets for every human clip, each batch draws human and robot clips in equal numbers, and robot clips are gathered across GPUs. We optimize with AdamW (learning rate 10−410^{-4}, β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.01) at a constant learning rate, with gradient clipping at 1.0 and bf16 mixed precision.

Policy.

The VLM is Qwen3-VL-4B, and the action expert is a separately parameterized Qwen3-style transformer with 0.6B parameters (36 layers, hidden size 768) that attends jointly with the VLM at every layer. The latent-action loss weight in equation 2.4 is λLA=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{LA}}=0.1. Pre-training starts from the Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct weights with a randomly initialized action expert and 8 latent queries; mid-training starts from the pre-trained checkpoint, and post-training from the mid-trained one, keeping the same architecture throughout.

9 Atomic-Action Annotations on RoboTwin 2.0

RoboTwin 2.0 collects expert trajectories by running a scripted program for each task with a motion planner (Chen et al., 2025b). The program composes the task from manipulation primitives, and the planner executes each primitive as a short sequence of arm motions and gripper commands. This execution divides each trajectory into atomic actions whose boundaries are given by the program. The program also specifies the target object and the executing arm of each atomic action, so we describe each atomic action in language without manual annotation. These atomic actions typically last about one second. Figure 12 shows one episode divided in this way. We annotate the ARX-X5 and Aloha-AgileX trajectories with the same procedure.

10 Real-World Platform

All real-world experiments use a Sharpa North robot11 1 https://www.sharpa.com/pages/north, a wheeled full-body humanoid with two 7-DoF arms, each equipped with a 22-DoF Sharpa Wave dexterous hand22 2 https://www.sharpa.com/pages/wave. The Wave is a human-scale, five-finger hand with a vision-based tactile sensor in each fingertip; our policy does not use tactile inputs. The policy observes RGB images from a head-mounted stereo camera and two wrist-mounted fisheye cameras, together with the joint angles of both arms, both hands, and five torso and neck joints. It predicts chunks of 32 joint-angle targets at 60 Hz, expressed relative to the current state and covering 63 actuated DoF, while images are captured at 30 Hz. Figure 13 shows the robot and its main components.

11 Real-World Tasks

For each task, we describe the goal and the success criterion. Figure 14 shows one teleoperated demonstration of each task.

Gear assembly.

The robot picks up three loose gears and assembles them onto the corresponding pegs of a base plate. A trial succeeds if all three gears are fully seated on the correct pegs with adjacent teeth engaged and remain in place after the robot releases them.

Bimanual pouring.

The robot transfers pills from a source cup into a receiving cup with both hands: one hand holds the receiving cup steady while the other lifts and tilts the source cup. A trial succeeds if all pills are transferred into the receiving cup without visible spillage and both cups are placed upright on the table and released.

Flower insertion.

The robot grasps a single flower by its stem, lifts it from a holder, and inserts the stem into a vase. A trial succeeds if the stem is inside the vase and the flower remains supported by the upright vase after the robot releases it.

Spoon scooping.

The robot picks up a spoon from its holder, scoops rice from a bowl, and pours a spoonful into a target cup. A trial succeeds if a spoonful of rice is deposited into the target cup without visible spillage outside the containers and the spoon is returned to its holder and released.
